clinicalPearls: Presents as sudden, painless, monocular visual loss; central retinal artery occlusion is an ocular equivalent of acute ischaemic stroke and warrants emergency stroke-pathway referral.
Fundoscopy classically shows a pale, oedematous inner retina with a cherry-red spot at the fovea; the arteriolar blood column may appear segmented (box-carring).
A relative afferent pupillary defect is usually present in central retinal artery occlusion.
In older patients, giant cell arteritis must be actively excluded as an arteritic cause that threatens the fellow eye.
Most emboli arise from carotid atherosclerosis or a cardiac source; a bright Hollenhorst (cholesterol) plaque may be visible at a bifurcation in branch occlusion.
Amaurosis fugax (transient monocular visual loss) is a warning of impending occlusion and a transient-ischaemic-attack equivalent.
A cilioretinal artery, when present, may perfuse and spare central macular vision despite central retinal artery occlusion.
Time is critical, as inner retinal neurons tolerate ischaemia only briefly before irreversible infarction.
reference.pathophysiology: The inner retina and retinal ganglion cells are supplied by the central retinal artery, a branch of the ophthalmic artery arising from the internal carotid artery, while the outer retina is nourished by the choroidal circulation. Acute occlusion, most often embolic (cholesterol, calcific or platelet-fibrin emboli), less commonly thrombotic, arteritic (giant cell arteritis) or vasospastic, produces abrupt ischaemia of the inner retinal layers. The ischaemic inner retina becomes oedematous and opacified, obscuring the underlying retinal pigment epithelium and choroid everywhere except the fovea, where the retina is thinnest and the intact choroidal blush shows through as the characteristic cherry-red spot. Because the choroid-dependent outer retina is relatively spared, some perception may persist. Branch occlusion produces a sectoral infarct and corresponding visual field defect. Prolonged ischaemia leads to irreversible neuronal death, later chronic inner retinal thinning, and occasionally neovascular sequelae.
additionalDifferentials: Arteritic and non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
additionalInvestigations: Optical coherence tomography (early inner retinal oedema, later inner retinal thinning)
Fluorescein angiography demonstrating delayed or absent retinal arterial filling
Urgent inflammatory markers and, where indicated, temporal artery biopsy to exclude giant cell arteritis
Carotid Doppler ultrasound and CT or MR angiography of the neck vessels
Transthoracic or transoesophageal echocardiography and ECG to seek an embolic cardiac source
Diffusion-weighted brain MRI, as concurrent clinically silent cerebral infarction is common
redFlags: Any accompanying neurological deficit suggesting concurrent cerebral stroke
Symptoms or signs of giant cell arteritis (jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, new headache, a tender or pulseless temporal artery)
Preceding amaurosis fugax indicating an impending stroke
Bilateral or simultaneous involvement, suggesting giant cell arteritis or an embolic shower
Ocular neovascularisation or features of the ocular ischaemic syndrome
reference.prognosis: Spontaneous visual recovery in central retinal artery occlusion is generally poor, whereas branch occlusion carries a better outlook depending on macular involvement. It is an important marker of systemic vascular disease, conferring a substantially raised risk of subsequent stroke and other cardiovascular events.
pitfalls: Missing giant cell arteritis and delaying corticosteroids while awaiting biopsy, thereby risking the fellow eye.
Managing it as an isolated eye problem rather than a stroke equivalent, and failing to refer urgently for vascular assessment.
Attributing sudden visual loss to migraine in an older patient.
Overlooking a carotid or cardiac embolic source on workup.
Misinterpreting foveal sparing by a cilioretinal artery and doubting the diagnosis.
management: Treat central retinal artery occlusion as an ocular stroke emergency with immediate referral to the acute stroke pathway, considering thrombolysis in hyperacute presentations at specialist centres

In the first hours attempt measures to dislodge the embolus and lower intraocular pressure, such as ocular massage, anterior chamber paracentesis and pressure-lowering agents, recognising limited evidence of benefit
Urgently exclude giant cell arteritis in older patients and, if suspected, start high-dose corticosteroids immediately to protect the fellow eye
Institute secondary prevention as for stroke with antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy, a statin, and control of blood pressure, diabetes and smoking
Investigate and treat the embolic source, including carotid endarterectomy for significant stenosis and management of any cardiac source
Monitor for ocular neovascularisation and treat with laser or anti-VEGF therapy if it develops
Coordinate care across stroke, ophthalmology and vascular services
